technique.how: After a brief cognitive test (e.g. months backwards, digit span) and interview, score four features: (1) acute onset and fluctuating course from an informant/chart, (2) inattention, (3) disorganized thinking, (4) altered level of consciousness. CAM positive = features 1 AND 2 plus either 3 or 4. Takes about 5 minutes.
technique.prerequisites: Baseline cognition from a collateral source; trained rater; patient able to respond (use CAM-ICU for intubated/non-verbal patients).

interpretation.positive_finding: Positive CAM makes delirium roughly 10 times more likely (pooled LR+ 9.6) and should trigger a search for the precipitant (infection, drugs, metabolic, withdrawal).
interpretation.negative_finding: Negative CAM lowers the probability substantially (pooled LR- 0.16) but pooled sensitivity is only ~0.82; repeat the screen if fluctuation is suspected.
interpretation.pitfalls: Accuracy falls with untrained raters and without a formal attention test; dementia, aphasia and hypoactive delirium lower sensitivity. The CAM identifies delirium, not its cause.
interpretation.changes_what: Positive: label as delirium and work up precipitants; negative: pursue dementia, depression, psychosis or focal neurology but rescreen if course fluctuates.

estimates.population: Hospitalized adults, mostly older medical/surgical inpatients, across 25 prospective studies (N=3027)
estimates.reference_standard: DSM-based diagnosis by geriatrician, psychiatrist or neurologist
estimates.quote: the CAM has the best available supportive data as a bedside delirium instrument (summary-positive LR, 9.6; 95% CI, 5.8-16.0; summary-negative LR, 0.16; 95% CI, 0.09-0.29)

estimates.population: Adults in a variety of medical settings; 22 studies of CAM and CAM-ICU (n=2442)
estimates.quote: The pooled sensitivities and specificity for CAM were 82% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 69%-91%) and 99% (95% CI: 87%-100%)
estimates.location: Abstract, Results; Results text and Figure 2 (bivariate estimate)

sources.citation: Wong CL, Holroyd-Leduc J, Simel DL, Straus SE. Does this patient have delirium?: value of bedside instruments. JAMA 2010;304:779-786.
Shi Q, Warren L, Saposnik G, Macdermid JC. Confusion assessment method: a systematic review and meta-analysis of diagnostic accuracy. Neuropsychiatr Dis Treat 2013;9:1359-1370.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Not a substitute for glucose, vitals, and focal neurological exam in acute mental-status change; use CAM-ICU in ventilated or non-verbal patients.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: A positive CAM with fever, meningism, focal deficit or reduced consciousness needs urgent evaluation for meningitis, stroke or sepsis regardless of screen result.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: RCE notes heterogeneity in LR confidence intervals across studies; accuracy depends on rater training and use of a structured cognitive assessment.

extraction_notes: Both pooled estimates are taken from abstracts (RCE full text and JAMA tables not accessible; Shi 2013 PMC full text confirmed the same numbers in Results and Figure 2). RCE per-study sens/spec table not visible, so sens/spec are cited from Shi 2013 rather than the RCE.
